section.title: Chapter review and applications
section.p: This chapter began with a sentence:
section.md: \text{A differential equation is a law written in the language of change.}
section.p: We have now seen several versions of that sentence.

A cooling cup obeys a law involving temperature difference. A population obeys a law involving current population and available capacity. A tank obeys a law involving inflow and outflow. A spring obeys a law involving displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Two populations can obey linked laws.
The methods differ, but the pattern is the same:
section.md: \text{model the rate, then understand the function.}

subsection.title: Skills: solve and interpret first-order equations
subsection.p: The first task in a differential equation is not to solve. It is to recognize what kind of equation is in front of us and what kind of answer is reasonable.

row.cell: What do solution curves seem to do?
Where are equilibria, and are they stable?
Can the variables be separated and integrated?
Can the product rule be used backward?
How does growth slow near carrying capacity?
How does a quantity approach a stable level?

subsection.p: The following examples review the central skills.

note.title: Review habit
note.p: After solving a differential equation, ask:

Does it satisfy the initial condition?
Does its long-term behavior match the model?

Were any solutions lost by division?

note.title: Model reflection
note.p: A differential equation is a simplified law. Real cups lose heat through the cup, the surface, evaporation, stirring, and changing room conditions. The model is useful because it captures the main pattern, not because it records every physical detail.

note.title: Project conclusion
note.p: A numerical method should be judged by both computation and behavior. A table of numbers is not enough. The numbers should agree with the direction field, the phase line, and any exact solution available.

exercise.title: What extra information turns a law of change into one history?

statement.p: A first-order equation usually needs one starting value; a second-order equation usually needs two. In your own words, why is that count part of the meaning of the model, not a bookkeeping afterthought?

hint.p: The law describes a family of possible motions. The starting state chooses which motion actually happens.

subsection.title: A final map of the chapter
subsection.p: The main ideas of the chapter can be summarized in one picture of dependencies.
and then we choose a route:

md.mrow: \text{modeling route} \amp:\quad \text{interpret constants, units, and long-term behavior}.

subsection.p: No one route is the whole subject. Often the best solution uses several at once.

For example, in a logistic model, the phase line tells us that a positive solution should approach K. The exact formula tells us when it reaches K/2. Euler’s method can approximate values when parameters are changing or when the equation becomes too complicated to solve exactly. The model interpretation tells us which values of P make physical sense.

note.title: What differential equations add to calculus
note.p: Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. Differential equations use those ideas to describe laws.

Differential equations often describe motion by using time as the input:
But many curves are not naturally graphs of the form

A point on a wheel, a planet moving in an orbit, or a particle tracing a loop may pass above the same x-value more than once. The curve may still be easy to describe if we let time trace both coordinates:
That is the next idea. Instead of forcing every curve to be a graph, we let a moving point draw it.

exercise.title: What do differential equations add to calculus?

statement.p: Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. In your own words, how do differential equations change the role of the derivative, and why does that turn an unknown function into the object we seek?

hint.p: The derivative becomes something we are given by a law, not only something we compute from a known formula.
